Why can’t I be steady? Why is my only balance built from the collisions and cancellations of such sharp, spike-of-chaos moods? A field of thistles, red and green. outputs.L2:
On May 23, 2010—Whitsuntide—a mountainside thistle patch sending out ring after ring of apophatic thought would provide that perpetually available yet rarely pursued condition of delicate astonishment, if only he shut down the computer and followed the road toward the summit until the ocean appeared. Perhaps the southeast wind carries broadcast data, too; perhaps the microsystem shares he has compulsively monitored and clicked through all day, like a gambling addict, will rise with it, their figures turning from red to green as they pass across the dark horizon. Two red-tailed hawks ascend on a thermal. You might even earn something while standing up here.

Why does every moment feel saturated with the sense that we are living through some deranged Götterdämmerung—an era ruled by the free-radical command to live or perish, by a negative white-on-white sun whose pride burns itself away—while at the same time brimming with a utopian, breakneck boast of endless life? Why can I never remain composed? Why does my sole form of equilibrium arise from violent moods, sharp eruptions of chaos that crash together and erase one another?

Thistles in red and green. Monetary fields—dollars and thistles, solidi, yen, rand, and rupees—lifting into the wind from the earth’s curved edge.

A field of thistles on a mountainside offers the speaker the possibility of a subtle spiritual awakening. Such a revelation, however, depends on the speaker’s willingness to leave the computer behind and walk toward the sea. The natural world promises a different form of attention—quiet, physical, and immediate—in contrast to the anxious vigilance demanded by the screen.

Yet the speaker remains absorbed in checking microsystems stocks, repeatedly hoping that losses displayed as red numbers will turn into profitable green gains. This obsessive financial speculation begins to shape the speaker’s perception of everything else. Even the sight of hawks rising effortlessly on a thermal becomes entangled with fantasies of upward market movement and sudden wealth. Nature is no longer entirely separate from the economy; its colors, patterns, and motions are interpreted through the language of profit and loss.

This confusion reflects the speaker’s unstable emotional state. The mind swings between apocalyptic dread and utopian optimism, imagining either complete collapse or miraculous success. The speaker questions why it is so difficult to remain emotionally steady between these extremes. In the final convergence of images, red and green thistles blend with the colors of stock-market figures and global currencies. Nature, money, and mood become part of the same volatile system, revealing a world in which spiritual longing is continually disrupted—and perhaps also intensified—by economic anxiety.
outputs.L4:
The speaker struggles to maintain emotional balance in a world defined by uncertainty. He is drawn compulsively to market movements, watching prices rise and fall as though each fluctuation might reveal what the future holds. Yet this attention offers no reassurance. Instead, the ceaseless flow of financial information intensifies his anxiety, linking private unease to broader fears of economic collapse, political disorder, and environmental catastrophe.

Against this atmosphere of dread, he imagines leaving the screens behind and walking across a mountainside covered in thistles. The landscape is rough rather than idyllic, but its physical immediacy provides a form of relief. The sharp plants, open slopes, and distant sea reconnect him with a world that exists beyond abstract numbers and predictions. In this imagined setting, movement itself becomes restorative: the act of walking suggests a temporary escape from paralysis and a return to bodily experience.

The vision does not eliminate fear, however. Its beauty remains entangled with the speaker’s awareness of disaster. The sea can appear peaceful and expansive, but it also evokes instability, danger, and forces beyond human control. Likewise, the thistles suggest resilience while retaining their capacity to wound. Nature therefore mirrors the speaker’s divided state, offering both consolation and reminders of vulnerability.

His fragile equilibrium depends on this collision between opposing impulses. Apocalyptic dread is countered by utopian hope—the possibility that another way of living might still be imagined, even if it cannot yet be reached. The speaker does not achieve serenity by denying volatility; instead, he finds a provisional balance by holding fear and hope together.

As the mountainside, sea, and financial markets begin to overlap symbolically, the distinction between the natural and economic worlds becomes unstable. Market graphs resemble shifting terrain or waves, while the landscape itself appears subject to the same forces of unpredictability and change. Through this merging of nature and global finance, the speaker creates an image of modern life as beautiful, interconnected, and dangerously volatile. His imagined walk offers no permanent refuge, but it gives him a momentary way to endure uncertainty and to envision renewal within it.
outputs.L5:
### May and Whitsuntide

May is a month of renewal. Trees are green again, gardens fill with flowers, and longer days invite people outdoors. The warmth of late spring brings a sense of hope and celebration.

Whitsuntide, also known as Pentecost, often falls in May or early June. In the Christian tradition, it commemorates the coming of the Holy Spirit and is associated with faith, unity, and new beginnings. Over time, Whitsuntide also became a season of public holidays, village festivals, family gatherings, and countryside walks.

May and Whitsuntide therefore share a joyful spirit. Both celebrate life in full bloom and offer an opportunity to pause, come together, and welcome the approaching summer.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, experimental prose poem about a man leaving his computer and stock-market screens to walk through thistles toward a mountain summit on Whitsuntide, blending negative theology, financial anxiety, hawks, and apocalyptic mood swings.
counterfactuals.output:
At Whitsuntide he shuts the blue lid on the markets—candlesticks guttering, futures chewing their red arithmetic, the little green arrows ascending without salvation—and leaves the room where every second has a price. Outside, thistles revise his trousers into blood. The mountain stands beyond disclosure, an unlisted silence, neither bullish nor bearish but terrible in its refusal to be named. He walks.

No cloud of tongues descends, only hawks circling the thermal like black signatures above a contract no body remembers signing. God is not the summit, he tells the stones. God is not the absence of the summit. God is not this breath leveraged against the next, nor the fear that somewhere his portfolio is collapsing beautifully, numbers unhousing numbers, panic selling panic. Each negation opens another mouth. Each mouth contains weather.

By noon the sky has upgraded him to euphoria: he could buy the valley, forgive the debt of rivers, ring every bell in the blood. By one, thunder enters the index. The hawks become auditors. The thistles flash their small purple catastrophes. He sees cities margin-called into flame, oceans lifting their dark balances, angels with scorched terminals crying SELL SELL SELL while the Spirit, if Spirit, arrives as a wind deleting passwords.

Higher: no reception. Higher: the self loses signal. His heart, that volatile exchange, surges, crashes, halts trading. He kneels among shale where nothing answers because answer is another idol, a coin stamped with the emperor’s vacancy. The mountain is not merciful. The mountain is not cruel. It does not know him, and this unknowing pours through him—white fire, blank dividend, Pentecost without language.

Below, his unattended screens continue manufacturing dawn and disaster.

Above, one hawk falls upward into the sun.

He rises into what cannot rise.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness passage set on May 23, 2010, in which a compulsive investor imagines market data drifting through a windswept landscape of thistles, sea views, and red-tailed hawks.
counterfactuals.output:
May 23, 2010—Sunday, markets closed, which only means the numbers have gone feral, escaped their grids and terminals to drift across the headland: 10,193.39 snagged in the thistles, the euro slipping downhill in pale decimals, crude oil flashing between blades of bent grass. Wind off the sea flattens my coat against my ribs. I should be watching the horizon, blue hammered into silver, but every whitecap resembles a chart breaking resistance, every gull a sell signal. Above the bluff, two red-tailed hawks circle without effort, buying the updraft, holding, holding, while I calculate what I could have made if I’d entered at the bottom, if the bottom was the bottom, if anything has a bottom anymore. The flash crash was seventeen days ago and still it flickers behind my eyes—liquidity vanishing like rain in sand, bids gone, the whole machine briefly admitting it was only wind.

Thistles nod their purple heads: diversify, diversify. My phone has no signal, yet I check it again. Asian futures will open while I sleep, assuming I sleep. Greece, Germany, contagion—the words blow past like torn financial pages. One hawk folds its wings and drops, a red tail burning against the sea, and my pulse jumps as if I’d placed the trade myself. Down, down, then the sudden correction, wings spread, loss arrested inches above the grass.

I tell myself this is why I came: salt air, silence, perspective. But the landscape keeps quoting prices. The rocks are undervalued. The clouds are overbought. The sea has infinite volume. And somewhere beyond Sunday, beyond the clean locked doors of the exchange, Monday is already assembling its columns of green and red, waiting for me to mistake hunger for foresight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a single-paragraph modernist prose poem that collides nature, mysticism, technology, global currencies, and manic-depressive thoughts. Use fragmented syntax, invented compounds, abrupt pronoun shifts, and occasional missing spaces.
counterfactuals.output: At dawn the river uploads its silver, reed-priests bending beneath a cloudserver psalm, and I—no, we, no one—wake bitcoin-bright, yen-winged, eurotrembling, convinced the sun has chosen my skull for its golden antenna; then noon cracks. A crow encrypts the oak. Moss whispers om,om through the fiber roots while dollars molt from the market-tree, rupees rain, pesos flicker in the throat of the ATM oracle. He runs—she burns—I become a thousand-tab prophet, clickblessed, thunderwired, naming every star and buying their futures; then theblack tide, sudden, no password, the moon a dead screen in the pines. Down into zero-country. Breath refuses its small machinery. Yet somewhere a fox moves like a red decimal through snow, and the buried cables hum their underworld mantra: rise/fall, loss/light, youarehereyouarenot, until morning reboots the wet leaves and we, briefly plural, touch the earth’s cold glass.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe a field of thistles on a mountainside as a source of “subtle shock,” while reflecting on negative theology, the stock market, ecological imagery, personal instability, and the tension between apocalypse and utopian longevity.
counterfactuals.output:
The thistles on the mountainside offered a subtle shock: not the violence of lightning, but the discovery that austerity could bloom. Their purple heads hovered above silver spines, a congregation devoted to a god best approached by subtraction—nameless, imageless, known through everything it refused to be.

Below, the market flickered on distant screens, green arrows and red losses pretending that panic had a grammar. Up here, value moved differently. Bees entered the blossoms; wind combed the dry grass; roots held a little soil against the long argument of erosion. Even ruin participated in nourishment.

I stood among them with my own life poorly staked—work uncertain, love provisional, the future rising and falling like a speculative share. The thistles did not console me. Their beauty kept its barbs. Yet that was the shock: the world’s tenderness had never promised safety.

The valley looked apocalyptic in the late red light, each ridge darkening as if rehearsing an ending. Still, seeds were already fastening themselves to the air. Perhaps utopia was not a perfected country beyond catastrophe, but this stubborn longevity: damaged ground inventing another season, life continuing without innocence, the thistle lifting its small, impossible crown.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intentionally difficult, lyrical, Joycean meditation beginning and ending with a field of thistles. Include Whitsuntide, a summit road overlooking the sea, red and green market numbers, two red-tail hawks, Götterdämmerung, and currencies blowing over the horizon.
counterfactuals.output:
A field of thistles, purple-pricked beneath the pewter weather, kept its innumerable small vigil: each thorn a compasspoint, each flower a bruised and bearded sun, while through their hooked parliament the wind went whispering—Whitsuntide, Whitsuntide—as though the year, having misplaced its tongue of fire, must borrow speech from weeds.

Upward he walked where the summit road, white-scarred and switchbacked, overlooked the sea. Below, immensities rehearsed their blue refusal. Villages lay like dropped crockery along the coves; roofs reddened, bells withheld themselves, smoke reasoned crookedly with heaven. He had climbed to outclimb what? The little inland usurer of the heart, perhaps, who keeps his red and green market numbers flickering behind the eyelids: gainloss, buybye, bloodleaf, the arithmetic of appetite. Red, the figures rose; green, they sank; or green they rose and red they sank, for value changes waistcoats while the poor coin sweats in every pocket.

Whitsuntide bells began somewhere unseen, not ringing so much as loosening circles in the air. Tongues of flame for fishermen, tongues of debt for merchants, tongues tongueless for him. And there—above the road’s last stone elbow—two red-tail hawks wheeled, one within the other’s widening thought, their pinions barely troubling the gale. Husband and wife? Murder and mercy? Two signatures signed by the sky upon a document no groundling could subpoena. Their cries fell keenly, cutting the sea into before and after.

He thought then of Götterdämmerung: not Wagner’s brassbound apocalypse alone, helmets blazing in the orchestral furnace, gods going down magnificently under invoices of fire, but the daily dusk of tinier deities. The god of the warm shopwindow. The god of tomorrow’s dividend. The domestic god who inhabits the blue cup until the cup breaks. All burning, all bargaining, while valkyrie winds rifled the exchanges and currencies blew over the horizon—dollars, drachmas, yen, pounds pale as mothwings, francs obsolete and ghostly, pesos cartwheeling, crowns without kings—each note fluttering its engraved promise toward a country made only of departure.

What wealth survives its weather? Gold drowns heavily. Paper escapes. Numbers, red and green, breed bodilessly in the electric dark. Yet the hawks possessed no purse but hunger, no kingdom but the turning air; and the sea, prodigal bankrupt, spent wave after wave upon the rocks and was never poorer.

Down in the hidden town bread was being divided, wine darkened in glasses, children came home with burrs in their socks. Pentecostal noon leaned westward. He stood where the summit road overlooked the sea and felt the wind pass through his ribs as through an abandoned harp, sounding neither grief nor gladness but their old intermarriage: grieflight, gladfall, the soul’s salt twilit syllable.

Then the two red-tail hawks parted, one seaward, one inland, and the whole high world seemed split between following and remaining. He descended without choosing. Behind him the currencies vanished beyond the blue ledge of sight; before him bells gathered the scattered air. Evening entered thorn by thorn, flower by flower, into a field of thistles.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
